titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §177: The Reproach to Wang Qan
about: One section, one speech. Chinggis sends two messengers, Arqai-Qasar and Sükegei-Jegün, to Wang Qan, the old ally he calls father, who has turned on him. The message is a reproach built from parts: the pledge never to believe the 'snake' of slander before a face-to-face hearing, the two-shafted cart that cannot move on one shaft, and a long reckoning of what each side has done for the other, from the Qan's killing of his brothers and his flight to the four heroes sent to rescue Senggum. The section ends, as printed, in the middle of a sentence; the messengers are sent off and the sentence is finished in §178. Much of the grammar is converbs hung on one verb, and the pronouns bi and či close the sentence to say who is acting.

sentences.t: Tende Uṅgirad-i oroγ̇uluγ̇ad odču Tüṅge γoroqan-u dorona baγ̇užu
sentences.l: There, the Ongirad (acc) making-enter, going, the Tünge little-river's east descending,
sentences.i: There he took the Ongirad in, went on, and halted east of the little river Tünge.
sentences.n: A converb chain: oroγ̇uluγ̇ad (-γ̇ad, 'having …-ed'), odču and baγ̇užu (-ču / -žu, '-ing') all hang on a main verb that does not arrive until baγ̇uba in the next unit, and the subject, Chinggis, is held back too. The Ming gloss for oroγ̇uluγ̇ad, 敎投入了 'made them cast themselves in', suggests the Ongirad were brought in or made to join; whether by force or by consent the text does not say. The 行 on Uṅgirad-i marks the accusative -i, not a dative. γoroqan here and γorqan in the next unit are one word, Ming (小)河 'little river'; the vowel in the first is Shiratori's spelling.

sentences.t: Čiṅgis Qaγan Arγai-Qasar-a Sügegei-Žeġün qojar-a daγ̇u bariγ̇ulurun Tüṅge γorqan-u dorona baγ̇uba.
sentences.l: Chinggis Qaγan, to Arγai-Qasar and Sügegei-Žeġün, to the two, the word making-hold-when, the Tünge little-river's east descended.
sentences.i: While Chinggis Qahan was charging Arqai-Qasar and Sükegei-Jegün with a message, he camped east of the Tünge stream.
sentences.n: -run is the converb 'when …-ing'. bariγ̇ulurun is bari- 'hold' + the causative -γ̇ul- + -run; the Ming gloss 把話 'hold the word' suggests 'made them take up (carry) the message'. daγ̇u itself is glossed only 敎 'cause'; I read it as daγu 'voice, word' because of 把話, but that is a guess. Arγai-Qasar-a and qojar-a are datives in apposition, 'to A and S, to the two'. The first finite verb, baγ̇uba, ends the chain begun in the last unit: Chinggis halts east of the Tünge. What the two are to say comes in the speech below.

sentences.t: Ebesün ber in-ü sain bolžuγ̇ui; aγtas man-u üjelebe.
sentences.l: Grass also its good has-become; geldings our grew-sturdy.
sentences.i: The grass had turned good as well, and our geldings had put on condition.
sentences.n: This is narration, saying why the camp was a good one, not yet the message. bolžuγ̇ui is bol- 'become' + -žuγ̇ui, a past with Ming 有: 'has become good'. in-ü is 'his, its' (Ming 他的), the third-person genitive set after its noun. aγtas is the plural of aγta 'gelding'; man-u 'our' is ba 'we' (Ming 俺, against bida 咱) in the genitive, stem man- plus -u. The verb üjelebe is the weak point: the Ming 荕節了 ('sinewed and jointed', i.e. 筋節) points to sturdiness or condition, which is what I give, tentatively; I do not otherwise know the stem.

sentences.t: "Qān ečige-de min-u ügüle" keġen ügülerün:
sentences.l: "Qan father-to my say" saying, speaking:
sentences.i: He told them, "Say to my father the Qan," and went on:
sentences.n: ügüle (the bare stem, Ming 說) is an imperative: 'Say (to him)!'. The quotation marks are Shiratori's: this short quote is the instruction to the two messengers, and the message itself opens in the next unit with a second quote. keġen is the converb 'saying (thus)' (ke(ġe)- 'say' + -n) and ügülerün 'while speaking'. min-u after ečige-de is the Ming 我的 'my'. Qān is here Wang Qan, whom Chinggis calls father throughout.

sentences.t: "Qān ečige min-u jaγ̇un čimar-tur nama ajuγ̇ulba či.
sentences.l: "Qan father my, what blame-in me frightened you."
sentences.i: "My father the Qan, what fault do you find in me that you have frightened me?
sentences.n: The message begins. The grammatical person is marked at the end of the sentence by the pronoun: či 'you' closes a verb in the second person (ajuγ̇ulba či, 'you frightened'), and bi 'I' does the same for the first. This runs through the whole speech, and each such či or bi is glossed as the pronoun it is printed as. jaγ̇un čimar-tur is 'in what blame' (Ming 甚麼 嗔怪裏); čimar 'blame, reproach' comes back at the end of the speech. ajuγ̇ulba is aju- 'fear' (Ming 怕) + the causative -γ̇ul- (Ming 敎) 'make afraid'; nama 'me' is the oblique form of bi, with the Ming 行 marking it as the object.

sentences.t: Ajuγ̇ulqu böġesü maγ̇un köġüd(i)-jen maγ̇un berined(i)-jen nuir qaṅγan jakin ülü ajuγ̇ulu či.
sentences.l: Frightening, if-it-be, bad sons-own, bad daughters-in-law-own, sleep having-sated, why not frighten you.
sentences.i: If there is frightening to be done, why do you not frighten your own wicked sons and wicked daughters-in-law, whom you let sleep their fill?
sentences.n: Two things to see. -ġesü, 'if, when' (Ming 呵), here böġesü: 'if it is a matter of frightening'. And ülü … ajuγ̇ulu, the negative ülü with the present-future, against ese with the past in the cart lines below: the project flags this pair. The Ming 行 on köġüd(i)-jen and berined(i)-jen marks the accusative; -jen is the reflexive 'one's own', referring to the subject, 'you'. The clause nuir qaṅγan is uncertain: Ming 睡 敎足了 'made sleep enough'. I take it as 'letting them sleep their fill' (safe, idle and unafraid); other readings are possible.

sentences.t: Deṅ saγ̇uqui iseri noγunidγažu deġegši γarqui huni dölüsgežü jakin tein ajuγ̇uluba či.
sentences.l: Deṅ sitting couch having-made-bow-low, upward rising smoke scattering, why so frightened you.
sentences.i: Why have you frightened in this way, bringing low the couch where one sits and scattering the smoke that goes up?
sentences.n: The picture: the couch where one sits (iseri, Ming 床) is brought low (noγunidγažu, Ming 敎低着 'made low') and the smoke that goes up (huni, 烟) is scattered (dölüsgežü, 散着) — a household ruined. I take it as an idiom for wrecking someone's home and fortunes, whom the fright falls on is not said in the Mongol (Chinggis himself, or the sons and daughters-in-law of the last unit), and the grammar does not decide. The sentence-opening Deṅ has no Ming gloss at all; I leave it unexplained (a particle, or a misprint).

to go out, come forth [出的]

sentences.t: Qān ečige min-u γalžirqu-ju küġün-e qadquγdaba či;
sentences.l: Qan father my, perhaps-sideways man-to were-stabbed you;
sentences.i: My father the Qan, were you perhaps jabbed from the side by some man,
sentences.n: Two parallel questions, this unit and the next, with the particle -ju / -jü (Ming 莫是 'is it perhaps that …', like maqa 'perhaps'). qadquγ̇daba is qadqu- 'stab' (Ming 搠 'thrust') + the passive -γ̇da- + -ba; the man is the doer, in the dative küġün-e (a dative can name the agent of a passive). The Ming 傍 'beside, at the side' gives the sense of γalžirqu; the word itself I cannot place. Jabbing and prodding are figures for being goaded on by someone, as the 'snake' lines below make plain.

sentences.t: kündeledü-jü küġün-e kökiġüldebe či.
sentences.l: Perhaps-crosswise man-to were-poked you.
sentences.i: or prodded crosswise by some man?
sentences.n: kündeledü (Ming 橫 'across, athwart') answers γalžirqu in the line above. kökiġüldebe: the stem is uncertain, the Ming 挑 means 'poke, goad'; passive -de- (the form after l) + -be. Both questions ask whether an outsider goaded the Qan against Chinggis, which the next lines make explicit.

sentences.t: Qān ečige min-u bida qojar jaγ̇u keġeldüleġei.
sentences.l: Qan father my, we two what did-speak-together?
sentences.i: My father the Qan, what did the two of us agree between us?
sentences.n: keġeldüleġei is ke(ġe)- 'say' + the reciprocal -ldü- 'one another' + -leġei, a past (Ming 了來). The reciprocal is the grammar to watch in these lines: the Ming glossators render it 共 'together'. bida 'we' is the inclusive 'you and I' (Ming 咱), and qojar 'two' stands after it. This is a question that the next lines answer.

sentences.t: Žorqalγun-u Hulaγ̇anuγ̇ud, Boldaγ̇ud-ta bida ese-ü ügüleldülüġei:
sentences.l: Žorqalγun's Hulaγ̇anuγ̇ud, at-Boldaγ̇ud we not-spoke-together?
sentences.i: At the Hula'anuud of Jorqalqun, at the Boldaqud, did we not speak together:
sentences.n: Three place names, each marked only 山名 'mountain': Žorqalγun-u (genitive, 'of'), Hulaγ̇anuγ̇ud, Boldaγ̇ud-ta (locative, 'at'). I take 'the Hulaγ̇anuγ̇ud (heights) of Žorqalγun' and then 'at the Boldaγ̇ud', but the punctuation does not decide how the three are joined. ese-ü ügüleldülüġei: ese 'not' with the past, and the question particle (the Ming puts 麽 on the verb): 'did we not speak together?'. The colon introduces what they said.

sentences.t: šüdütü moγaj-a südürteġesü südürgen- dür in-ü bu oroja;
sentences.l: Tooth-having snake-to if-incited, in-instigation his not let-us-enter;
sentences.i: If the fanged snake incites us, let us not be drawn into his instigation;
sentences.n: šüdütü (Shiratori's š) is südü 'tooth' + -tü 'having' (Ming 牙有的): the tooth-having snake is the one who incites and sows discord, as the lines that follow say. südürteġesü is südür- 'incite' (Ming 挑唆 'stir up trouble') + the passive -te- + -ġesü 'if' (Ming 被挑唆呵). südürgen- / dür is one word split by the printed hyphen: 'in the instigation' (Ming 挑唆 時 'at the time of'). moγaj-a is the dative of the doer, 'by the snake' (as küġün-e above). bu is the prohibitive 'do not' and oroja 'let us enter' (-ja the hortative).

sentences.t: südü-ġer ama-γ̇ar olulčažu büšireje ese-ü keġeldüleġei.
sentences.l: Tooth-with, mouth-with having-confronted-each-other, let-us-trust; not did-speak-together?
sentences.i: Face to face, tooth to tooth and mouth to mouth, let us trust one another: did we not agree so?
sentences.n: südü-ġer ama-γ̇ar: the instrumental -ġer / -γ̇ar 'with, by', in the two vowel forms (front after südü, back after ama). 'Tooth and mouth' is each side speaking to the other, face to face. olulčažu: Ming 對證着 'confronting, checking against one another'; I take the stem to be olu- 'find' + -lča- 'together' (uncertain). büšireje is büšire- 'trust' (Ming 信) + -je 'let us'; the same verb appears below as 'to be grateful' (Ming 知感). ese-ü keġeldüleġei closes the unit with the question, as at the start of the pledge.

sentences.t: Edöġe Qān ečige min-u südü-ġer ama-γ̇ar-u olulčažu qaγačaba či.
sentences.l: Now Qan father my, with-tooth with-mouth confronting, did-you-part?
sentences.i: Now, my father the Qan, after we confronted each other tooth to tooth and mouth to mouth, have you broken away?
sentences.n: qaγačaba is qaγača- 'part, separate' (Ming 分離). The Ming 麽 on ama-γ̇ar-u marks the question, which is how I take the sentence. The literal run is 'by tooth, by mouth, having confronted, have you parted?'; I keep that order, so 'having confronted' is not turned into 'broken from confronting'. Whether the point is a broken pledge the text leaves to the reader.

sentences.t: Qān ečige min-u bi čuġen ber böġesü olon-(n)i ülü eriġülkü büleġe.
sentences.l: Qan father my, I little even-if-be, much (acc) not made-seek was.
sentences.i: My father the Qan, even when I had little, I never made you hunt for more;

The Ming 敎尋 is 'cause to seek'. Who is made to seek is not said; I take it to be the Qan. ber böġesü 'even if it be' (ber 'also, even'): 'even if (it was) little' — little of what, the text leaves open (strength, goods).

sentences.t: Ölesügsen-i čin-u üdür düli-de ese kürgebe-že;

sentences.i: I did not let your hunger last until the noon of a day,
sentences.n: The Ming 敎到 for kürgebe is 'cause to arrive'. sentences.i: Next morning, when I looked and your camping-place was empty, I thought: "You have been moved off, and these people have been making a cooked meal of us."
sentences.n: boldarun: bol- + the passive -da- + -run (Ming 被做時 'when made'): 'when it came to be (without)'. ködöldežü: ködöl- 'move' + the passive -de- + -žü (Ming 被動着 'being moved'). edeči (Ming 這的每) is 'these people', with a plural ending I cannot separate. tülešilen (Ming 做燒飯 'make cooked rice') is the weak point: the glossary already carries it as 'a cooked meal' (§161), and I keep that, 'making a cooked meal of us', without 'burnt'; the idiom is not known to me, and whether it points back to the fires left burning in the unit above I cannot tell. Who 'these' are (the Qan's men, I think) is not told either. keġežü 'saying' I give as 'I thought'. The (i)-jan of baidal-dur(i)-jan 'own' looks back to the Qan (čima-ji), not to the speaker; I take it as 'his own camp'.

sentences.t: Köġün min-u dörben külüġü- d(i)-jen ögčü ire keġežü ireġesü čin-u metü ülü sedkin tende bi.
sentences.l: Son my, four heroes-own having-given come saying, when-came, your like not thinking there, I.
sentences.i: When you sent word, "My son, give your four heroes and let them come here," I did not think as you think now.
sentences.n: A choice of reading. -jen 'one's own' refers to the person addressed, so köġün min-u 'my son!' is the Qan's address to Chinggis and dörben külüġüd-i-jen 'your own four heroes' are Chinggis's paladins; ögčü ire is 'give (them) and let (them) come' (ire the bare stem 'come!', Ming 來, not the 敎來 of the closing lines), and ireġesü 'when (the call) came'. čin-u metü is 'like yours', ülü sedkin 'not thinking', tende bi 'I, then'. The Ming gives külüġü as 傑 'hero'; the word is split by the hyphen (külüġü- / d(i)-jen).

sentences.i: I mustered armies and sent them out with these four heroes — Bo'orchu, Muqali, Boroqul and Chila'un, the brave men — each with his own men,
sentences.n: baγ̇atur 'hero, brave man' (Ming 勇士) stands in apposition to the four names. külüġüd(i)-jer(i)-jen is külüġü + the plural -d + the instrumental -(i)jer 'with' + the reflexive -jen 'own', in a pile of Shiratori's bracketed (i)s: 'with their own'; I read 'with their own men'. The Ming glossators do not separate the elements. ileġesü (Ming 去呵) is ile- 'send' + -ġesü: 'when I sent'.

sentences.t: Čimarun josun-dur elčin ire;
sentences.l: Blame's principle-in envoy make-come;
sentences.i: If you have grounds for reproach, send envoys;
sentences.n: Čimarun is čimar 'blame' with the genitive -un, and josun is 'principle, ground' (Ming 道理): 'the grounds of blame'. ire carries the Ming 敎來 'cause to come' and takes accusative objects in the lines below (qojar-i, nögöži-ji), so I read it as 'make come, send', though the form shows no causative suffix; a plain imperative 'come!' would not govern an accusative.
